title: Everything anyone asked for, between 1961 and now
client: A national library, acting through its head of collections and a fundraising office that reports to a separate director. The two have not agreed on anything in eight months and are both signatories.
event: Since 1961 the library has kept every completed reader request slip: the shelfmark, the seat number, the date, and the reader's own handwriting. There are about 2.1 million of them in forty-two steel drawers on a floor that is being given over to plant. The board voted four to two to pulp them and the contract is signed for 14 January.
when: The drawers are emptied on 14 January. The vote was in June and will not be revisited.
where: The entrance hall of the library, which is a thoroughfare rather than a destination, and where nobody has ever stopped for anything.
function: Say that this is being destroyed, before it is, in a building most of whose users have no idea it exists. It has worked if a reader who has never thought about the request they filled in an hour ago understands that the record of it is about to end. It has not worked if it reads as the library congratulating itself on its own history.
audience: Readers coming in and going out, about nine hundred a day, most of them in a hurry and most of them under thirty. Staff, many of whom filed these slips. Four members of the board who voted to destroy them and will walk past it.
production: The library's own workshop, which does the exhibition captions and has one process it is confident in. Two weeks in December between other jobs.
quantity: Six, at the size the workshop can handle, for the hall and the two stair landings.
budget: Internal only, which means the workshop's materials and no cash, and the head of collections has been told not to ask for more.
timeline: Installed by 8 December, so it stands for the five weeks before the drawers are emptied.
clientWantThatHurtsTheWork: The fundraising office requires that the endowment which paid for the floor conversion be named, at a size it has specified, because the same endowment is being asked for the next thing.

Reader confidentiality removes the only specific material there is. No shelfmark, no date belonging to an identifiable request, nothing that could be traced to a person. The handwriting is what makes the slips worth keeping and none of it can be shown.
The head of collections wants it understood that she voted against, and has asked for the vote to be recorded as four to two rather than as a decision of the board.
Legal will not permit the word destroyed. The approved term is deaccessioned, which nobody outside the building understands.
clientFear: That readers will start a campaign, that the campaign will fail because the contract is signed, and that the library will have spent its credit with the people who use it on a fight it already lost in June.
stakes: Nothing that happens here changes the date. The slips go on 14 January whatever this does. What is at stake is whether the last sixty-five years of the library's actual use is noticed by anyone before the record of it stops existing, and whether the institution is seen to have said so itself or to have been caught.

hard_constraints.why: The span is the only argument. A record kept without a break since a stated year is a different claim from a pile of paper in a basement.
Confidentiality has taken every particular away, so quantity is the entire remaining description of what is being lost.
Without the date this is a lament. With it, it is a notice, and the five weeks it stands are five weeks that are running out.

notes: The workshop foreman has offered to keep one drawer at his own house. Nobody has said yes and nobody has said no.
